title: runtime-topology-stability-index-and-degradation-simulation-2027
author: Priya Desai
content:
Overview
-------
This page defines our Runtime Topology Stability Index (RTSI), the accompanying Degradation Simulation framework, and operational playbooks for using these signals to guide kernel scheduling decisions, profiling campaigns, and benchmark validation. The goal is to provide a reproducible method for quantifying how a runtime topology (sharding, KV cache layout, kernel variants, and scheduler policies) reacts to progressive stress and to capture early warnings before user-visible SLO degradation.

Why this exists
 - We frequently ship scheduler and kernel changes that affect tail latency and fidelity in subtle ways; unit tests and microbenchmarks are insufficient.
 - RTSI provides a single, actionable score tied to observability signals and a simulation harness to stress topologies in controlled ways.
 - The output informs rollout gating: canaries, weighted rollouts, and automated fallback thresholds in the router.

Scope
 - Applies to all Hosted and Dedicated runtime topologies. Private deployments should re-run the simulation with local traffic shapes.
 - Focuses on inference-serving concerns: latency quantiles, error rates, memory pressure, shard-eviction churn, kernel-failure propagation, and KV cache warmup dynamics.

Definitions
 - Topology: placement of model shards, KV cache shards, and scheduler domains across GPUs and nodes.
 - RTSI: scalar 0–100 where 100 is fully stable under synthetic and replayed traffic stress; lower scores indicate increasing instability.
 - Degradation Mode: class of graceful-fallback or failure (e.g., soft-fidelity degradation, eviction storm, kernel stall).

RTSI design and signals
----------------------
RTSI is computed from a weighted aggregation of normalized signals collected during a simulation run:
1) Latency head/tail scores (p50, p95, p99) — directionally prioritized to penalize tail shifts.
2) Error amplification factor — rate of increased 5xx/response-timeouts vs baseline.
3) Eviction churn index — rate of KV/shard evictions per minute and the time-to-warm (cold-hit penalty).
4) Kernel slip events — frequency of kernel slow-path engagements and soft-fallback triggers.
5) Cross-cohort interference — latency correlation coefficient across tenant cohorts.
6) Recovery velocity — time for metrics to return to baseline after load drop or mitigation (seconds).

Weighting and normalization
 - Default weights: tail latency (0.35), error amplification (0.20), eviction churn (0.15), kernel slip (0.15), cohort interference (0.10), recovery velocity (0.05).
 - Signals are normalized to 0..1 where 0 is worst-case observed in historical incidents and 1 is baseline. RTSI = 100 * weighted_sum(normalized_signals).
 - The weight set is configurable per release; changes must be reviewed with SRE and runtime leads.

Degradation Simulation Framework (how to run)
-------------------------------------------
Purpose: execute deterministic experiments combining synthetic bursts and replayed production traces to surface interaction effects across layers (scheduler, kernel, cache).
Prereqs:
 - Access to the simulation harness (git: infra/runtime-sim) and a small cluster configured with the topology under test.
 - An anonymized request trace (see trace-redaction-playbook) or the synthetic suite.
 - Baseline golden metrics for the model/sequence distribution.

Quick run (smoke):
1) Checkout infra/runtime-sim@stable and configure experiment.yaml (example below).
2) Start cluster: ./scripts/sim-cluster up --topology topology.json --nodes 4
3) Load baseline: ./scripts/load-baseline --trace traces/golden-corpus.json 
4) Run progressive storm: ./scripts/run-storm --burst-factor 3 --duration 600 --cohorts 3
5) Collect artifacts: ./scripts/collect-artifacts --out /tmp/sim-output
6) Compute RTSI: python tools/compute_rtsi.py --input /tmp/sim-output --weights config/weights.yaml

Example experiment.yaml:
| name | value |
| experiment_name | rtsi-sanity-2027 |
| topology_file | topologies/4node-nonuniform.json |
| trace | traces/median-length-100.json |
| burst_pattern | step(1,3,30m) |
| scheduler_profile | econ-priority-governor-v2 |
| kernel_variants | [tf32, int8-fallback] |

Kernel-scheduling interaction checklist
--------------------------------------
When scheduling policy changes are proposed, run the following minimal checklist against RTSI:
1) Local pressure test: simulate single-node degradation and measure eviction churn and kernel slip.
2) Cross-node blast: multi-cohort ramp to expose interference.
3) Fallback exercise: intentionally trigger a kernel slow-path and validate graceful fallback latency bound.
4) Canary schedule: run weighted rollout simulation with 5/25/70 split and verify RTSI delta <= 6 points.

Profiling playbook (collection guidance)
-------------------------------------
Signals to collect during simulation runs:
 - Latency histograms (per-cohort, per-model) with 1ms bins up to 2s.
 - Kernel telemetry: kernel-id, path (fast/slow), elapsed_ns, occupancy, tensor shapes.
 - KV cache metrics: hits, misses, evictions, warmup-latency per key-range.
 - Node-level: GPU-util, memory_used, page_faults, temperature, nvlink-errors.
 - Scheduler: slot-queue-length, per-priority utilization, preemptions, admission denials.

Data retention and sample rates:
 - For simulation runs keep full traces and kernel telemetry for 30 days. Aggregates (per-minute) are retained for 90 days.
 - Use stratified sampling for long runs: preserve all p99 contributors and sample head requests at 1% to save storage.

Benchmarking suite integration
-----------------------------
RTSI is integrated into the acceptance benchmark suite:
 - Pre-merge checks run a lightweight sim (10m, small cluster) and verify RTSI >= 85 for low-risk backports.
 - Release gates run extended sims (2–6 hours) on release branches; failures (RTSI delta > 10 vs baseline) block signoff.
 - Benchmark artifacts include an artifacts manifest with: topology.json, scheduler_policy.yaml, kernel_build_hash, raw traces, and computed RTSI report.

Release notes and versioning
---------------------------
When a runtime change modifies scheduling or kernels, release notes must include:
 - RTSI baseline and delta observed in extended sim runs.
 - Kernel variant compatibility table and roll-forward/rollback instructions.
 - Recommended canary matrix (percentages, duration, SLOs to watch).
 - Any config toggles to delay rollout (feature flags) and their default state.

Known issues and interpretations
-------------------------------
We surface deterministic patterns that should not be treated as immediate blockers but require follow-up: 
 - Eviction ripple: small increases in eviction rate that grow over minutes indicate mis-sized KV partitions. Triage: re-evaluate shard sizing and prefetch hints.
 - Kernel slip noise: intermittent slow-path entries isolated to particular tensor shapes. Triage: add microbench for the shape and consider kernel specialization.
 - Inter-cohort correlated tails: events where a small tenant induces p99 increases across unrelated cohorts — typically scheduler admission quanta or quota shaping misconfig.

Operational runbooks (step-by-step)
---------------------------------
Runbook A: RTSI regression detected during CI
1) Abort the merge and alert runtime-sre@redwood.
2) Attach artifacts manifest and full sim output to the ticket.
3) Triage: run quick delta profiler (scripts/quick-delta) to localize to scheduler/kernel/cache.
4) If kernel suspected, run kernel smoke on microbench harness and isolate commit.
5) If scheduler suspected, revert policy or reduce canary weight and re-run sim.
6) Update the release notice with root cause and mitigation.

Runbook B: Production tail-latency spike suspected to match simulation signature
1) Toggle circuit-breaker: route traffic to fallback model-variant.
2) Open incident, tag with simulation label and link to last successful RTSI run.
3) Run targeted replay for the last 10 minutes using production trace sampler.
4) If RTSI-like signature reproduced, follow kernel rollback path.
5) If not reproduced, escalate to SRE/runtime-engineering for deeper tracing.

Ownership and governance
-----------------------
 - Primary owner: Runtime Architecture (runtime-arch@redwood).
 - SRE for policy: eng-sre (oncall rotation).
 - Profiling and kernel analysis: Performance and Applied ML teams.
 - Changes to RTSI formula or default weights require: runtime-arch + eng-sre + perf signoff.

Appendix A — Example weight file (config/weights.yaml)
---
# weights.yaml
tail_latency: 0.35
error_amp: 0.20
eviction_churn: 0.15
kernel_slip: 0.15
cohort_interference: 0.10
recovery_velocity: 0.05

Appendix B — Troubleshooting checklist (fast)
 - p99 spiked but p95 stable: check kernel slip histogram and tail shapes.
 - Eviction count rising: check partition distribution and hot-key lists.
 - One-node pressure causing cross-node tails: investigate slot reservation and NUMA bindings.
